newsitem.title: UK: Soviet-style queues live on at EBRD meeting.
newsitem.headline: Soviet-style queues live on at EBRD meeting.

text.p: Bankers spent hours in Soviet-style queues on Saturday as they waited to register for a meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, prompting the bank to offer rebates to hundreds of participants.

The embarrassing bottleneck at a converted brewery in the City of London, which the EBRD is using for some events at this year's annual meeting, meant some delegates missed key presentations as they waited for more than five hours to pick up high-tech passes.

"This was the only thing I was interested in seeing today and I missed it," said Eeva Juujarvi of Finnish telecommunications consultants Omnitele, after being admitted several hours too late for a telecoms workshop.
She arrived around 9 a.m. for the 10 a.m. event but only got in around 2.30 p.m. Her story was typical of many.
Ironically, the EBRD meeting centres on the efforts of former communist countries in central and eastern Europe to develop more efficient "western-style" economies.
A Baltic government minister took one look at the line, muttered "Screw this" and hailed a cab.
"I have attended the African Development Bank in Brazzaville and I have never experienced anything like this," said one irate banker after spending three hours in a queue with two colleagues.
"Think how much that cost," he added.

Journalists were left in the snaking queue until a bank official remembered their badges had been prepared in advance. However, some reporters still queued for hours, unaware that they could have gone straight through.
The EBRD, which was created in part to demolish Soviet-style economies in which long queues for just about anything were commonplace, later apologised for the foul-up.
"The only thing I can do is to offer my apologies," EBRD secretary general Antonio Costa told reporters.

The bank issued a statement offering to refund the 200 pound ($320) registration fee for those who registered in the four hours when the queue was at its worst, and to waive the fees for anyone who had to accept a temporary badge.
"I expect perhaps 400 people to apply," Costa said, acknowledging that this was perhaps the worst administrative mess in the controversial bank's history.
He said the lines were partly a result of delays in preparing identity badges and of the difficulties in finding a suitable venue in London for a conference of 4,500 people.
The need for high security in a city on full alert for possible bomb attacks by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) during Britain's election campaign also slowed things down.
The London Marathon, expected to attract 27,000 runners and more than half a million spectators on Sunday, could give organisers further headaches as many access roads may be closed.

The EBRD annual meeting and associated events continue until Tuesday and are split between three sites. More than 1,000 participants tried to register on Saturday and pick up passes with photographs and security bar codes.
"This is the third annual conference I have organised and the first two went smoothly," Costa said.
Some veterans of the EBRD conference circuit agreed. "I went to the conference in St Petersburg two years ago and the Russians organised it really well."
The EBRD, set up in 1991 to help Soviet bloc countries in the transition to market economies, has had a controversial past.
Its first president, Frenchman Jacques Attali, had to resign in 1993 after being criticised for his role in the 66 million pound ($107 million) fitting-out of its London headquarters.
